# Critical Path Method

The longest chain of dependent tasks through a network, and therefore the shortest possible project
duration. Tasks on it have zero float: slip one and the finish date moves by exactly that amount.
Tasks off it have slack and can absorb delay silently.

In [[computer-project-management]] the critical path is not computed by hand — it is read off
Microsoft Project's own critical flag and rendered in the tracking Gantt, ten tasks long:

> "Ten tasks lie on the critical path — any slip on these moves the finish date directly."
> — Computer Project Management/README.md, 2026-07-10

From the June reporting date onward it runs *integration testing → user-acceptance testing →
deployment → documentation → closure*.

## Why it is the concept the repo actually demonstrates

The plan's headline number is an 11-day slip, and the critical path is the mechanism that produces
it. Unit testing was extended by 16 days; the finish moved by 11. The two numbers differ because
part of the extension was absorbed by float elsewhere and part propagated — which is the whole
content of the method. See [[schedule-baseline-and-variance]] for the arithmetic.

The path is also **created**, not merely observed. Re-linking integration testing to start *after*
unit testing rather than in parallel puts both tasks on one chain, and that chain became the
critical one — [[sequence-integration-after-unit-testing]]. A scheduling decision taken to fix a
resource conflict changed the network topology, and the finish date followed.

## Relation to the other two levers

| Lever | Moves the finish date by | Instance here |
|---|---|---|
| Decomposition | changing what the chain is made of | [[work-breakdown-structure]] — 38 → 45 tasks |
| Resourcing | forcing overlapping tasks apart | [[resource-leveling]] — 110 d → 121 d |
| Sequencing | changing dependency type or order | [[sequence-integration-after-unit-testing]] — 123 d → 134 d |

Only the third one is a free choice; the first two are consequences.

## What is missing

- **No float or slack figures anywhere.** The critical path is reported as a task list; the near-critical
  tasks — the ones that would become critical next — are never identified.
- **No PERT or three-point estimation.** Durations are single-point. There is no probabilistic
  finish date and no schedule risk analysis in any readable file.
- **No crashing or fast-tracking analysis.** Once the slip appeared it was accepted and reported;
  no compression alternative is costed. `TODO:` unrecorded, not asked at interview.
- **`confidence: medium`** — the ten-task claim exists only as prose in the READMEs and a red-bar
  screenshot. No exported task list confirms it, and the `.mpp` files are unread by policy.
